To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the audiovisual modally was faster and more accurate than the auditory modally, and that the manual response was less accurate in noise than the oral one, which is consistent with the idea that a rough motor representation is evoked during the first stage of processing, and is refined during a second stage.

(1) auditory and visual speech information is integrated before the final decision, (2) the integration of the two streams is more efficient in the presence of noise than in the absence of noise and (3) the integration is not influenced by the type of motor response (oral vs manual).

(1) auditory close-shadowing is a fast and accurate speech task; (2) manual close-shadowing is less accurate in noisy conditions; (3) audiovisual close-shadow- ing is faster and more accurate than auditory close-shadowing in noisy conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the role of motor processes in speech perception.
the role of the motor representations in speech perception and production.
the study of speech processing and more precisely with the role of the motor component in speech perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the motor system is not involved in speech perception, but rather in the decision process.
the motor system is involved in speech perception, but only in a very specific and limited way, namely when a decision has to be taken.
the motor system is involved in speech perception, but not necessarily in a direct way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the auditory and visual modalities can interact with each other at different stages, depending on the task and the context.
the motor system is engaged early in the speech processing stream, but it is not necessarily the only one to be involved in the final decision.
the motor system is engaged in the processing of speech stimuli, but that this does not necessarily lead to a motor-compatible representation of the speech input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the context of close-shadowing, the visual input can speed up the response, but it does not seem to be used to shape the motor response.
the motor system can be engaged by both auditory and visual modalities, and that it can be modulated by the acoustic context.
the motor system may be involved in speech perception at a relatively late stage, when the auditory and visual inputs have been integrated.
